title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: A model only knows what's in its prompt. Retrieval is the mechanism that decides, out of everything you could put there, which pieces actually get in, by searching, not by hoping the right chunk made the cut.
objectives: Explain why retrieval exists: the gap between "in the prompt" and "known by the model"
Describe what an embedding is and why cosine similarity measures relevance, not magnitude
Explain the role of a minimum-relevance threshold, and why "closest available" isn't always "relevant"
Implement cosine similarity and top-k retrieval over a small in-memory document set

hints.title: Hint 1: conceptual
hints.mdx: Break it into two pieces: a helper that scores one query vector against one document vector, and a second step that scores every document, filters, sorts, and slices. Don't try to do all four at once in one loop.

hints.title: Hint 2: specific
hints.mdx: Cosine similarity of vectors a and b: dot product divided by (magnitude of a times magnitude of b). Dot product is the sum of `a[i] * b[i]` across matching indices. Magnitude is the square root of the sum of each vector's own squared components (Python's `math.sqrt`).

hints.title: Hint 3: near-solution
hints.mdx: If either magnitude is 0 (a zero vector), return a score of 0 immediately for that pair, don't divide by zero. After scoring every document, filter out anything with `score < min_score`, sort the rest descending by score using `sorted(..., key=..., reverse=True)`, then slice with `[:k]`.

tests.name: Results are ranked by similarity, exact match scores highest and sorts first
tests.hint: Sort your scored documents descending by score. The document with vector [1,0] against query [1,0] should score 1.0 and come first.

tests.name: Cosine similarity ignores vector magnitude (scale-invariant)
tests.hint: Divide the dot product by the product of both vectors' magnitudes. [1,0] and [5,0] point the same direction, they should both score ~1.0 against a [1,0] query, regardless of length.

tests.name: min_score excludes low-relevance documents even when k allows more
tests.hint: Filter out any scored document with score < min_score BEFORE slicing to k. Document B (opposite direction, score -1) should be excluded when min_score is 0, even though k=5 would otherwise have room for it.

tests.name: k limits output to the top-k highest scores, regardless of input order
tests.hint: Score every document first, then sort the FULL scored list descending, THEN slice to k. Slicing before sorting (or sorting the wrong direction) gives the wrong top-k.

tests.name: A zero-length document vector scores 0 and never raises or produces NaN
tests.hint: Before dividing by the product of magnitudes, check if either magnitude is 0. If so, return a score of 0 for that pair instead of dividing by zero.

questions.question: Query vector \[1, 0\] compared against document vector \[0, 5\]. What's the cosine similarity?

numeric.correct: Correct. [1,0] and [0,5] are perpendicular, cosine similarity is 0.
numeric.incorrect: Not quite. [1,0] and [0,5] are perpendicular (90°), cosine similarity of perpendicular vectors is always 0.

questions.question: Query vector \[3, 4\] compared against document vector \[6, 8\] (same direction, double the length). What's the cosine similarity?

numeric.correct: Correct. [6,8] is exactly [3,4] scaled by 2, same direction, so cosine similarity is 1, magnitude is irrelevant.
numeric.incorrect: Not quite. [6,8] points in the exact same direction as [3,4] (it's just scaled by 2), so cosine similarity is 1.

questions.question: Why does cosine similarity divide out vector magnitude instead of just using raw dot product as the score?

options.text: Because magnitude reflects the vector's length, not how semantically related the underlying texts are
options.why: Dividing out magnitude leaves a pure measure of direction, which is what corresponds to semantic similarity.

options.text: Because dot product is too slow to compute for large vectors
options.why: That's not the reason, dot product is actually a component of cosine similarity itself, and isn't meaningfully slower. The issue is what raw dot product means, not how fast it runs.

options.text: Because raw dot product can never be negative
options.why: Raw dot product can absolutely be negative, for vectors pointing in opposing directions. That's not the reason magnitude gets divided out.

questions.principle: Dividing out magnitude leaves a pure measure of direction, which is what corresponds to semantic similarity.

questions.question: A retrieval system with k=5 and no minimum-score threshold is asked a question totally unrelated to anything in its document collection. What does it return?

options.text: Its 5 best-scoring documents anyway, even though none of them are actually relevant
options.why: Without a minimum-relevance threshold, top-k always returns k results, whatever scored highest, relevant or not.

options.text: An empty result set automatically, since nothing matches well
options.why: Not automatically, top-k without a threshold has no concept of 'not good enough,' it always returns exactly k results (or fewer if the collection has less than k documents), ranked by whatever scored highest, relevant or not.

options.text: An error, since no document scores above a reasonable relevance level
options.why: No error, similarity scoring doesn't know what 'reasonable' means without an explicit threshold, it just returns the mathematically highest-scoring k documents.

questions.principle: Without a minimum-relevance threshold, top-k always returns k results, whatever scored highest, relevant or not.

questions.question: A RAG system retrieves 3 chunks (400 tokens total) for a query, then sends them plus the user's question (50 tokens) to a model with an 8000-token context window and 1000 tokens reserved for output. Using Module 2's terms, is this call anywhere near the input budget limit?

options.text: No, it's well under budget: 450 tokens used against a 7000-token available input budget (8000 window − 1000 output)
options.why: 400 (chunks) + 50 (question) = 450 input tokens, against a 7000-token available budget, plenty of headroom.

options.text: Yes, it's already over budget since retrieval adds tokens on top of the question
options.why: 450 total input tokens is far below the 7000-token available input budget, adding retrieved chunks does add tokens, but this specific call is nowhere near the limit.

options.text: It's impossible to tell without knowing the exact tokenizer used
options.why: This course's planning estimate (or any reasonable estimate) is precise enough here, 450 tokens against a 7000-token budget isn't a borderline case that needs exact tokenizer precision to evaluate.

questions.principle: 400 (chunks) + 50 (question) = 450 input tokens, against a 7000-token available budget, plenty of headroom.

questions.question: Query vector [0, 1] compared against document vector [1, 0]. What's the cosine similarity?
questions.objective: Compute cosine similarity for perpendicular vectors

options.text: 0, the vectors are perpendicular
1, both vectors have the same magnitude
options.why: Magnitude being equal doesn't make vectors similar in direction, these two point in completely different directions (90° apart), giving a similarity of 0.

options.text: -1, the vectors are opposite
options.why: Opposite vectors would be [1,0] and [-1,0], these two are perpendicular, not opposite, perpendicular gives 0, not -1.

questions.question: Why does cosine similarity ignore vector magnitude?

options.text: Magnitude reflects length, not how semantically related two pieces of text are, dividing it out leaves a pure measure of direction (meaning)
Because computing magnitude is too computationally expensive
options.why: Magnitude is trivial to compute (a square root of a sum of squares), the reason it's divided out is about MEANING, not computational cost.

options.text: It doesn't, cosine similarity is affected by magnitude just like dot product is
options.why: This is exactly backwards, cosine similarity is specifically defined to divide out magnitude, that's what distinguishes it from raw dot product.

questions.question: Top-k retrieval with k=5 and no minimum-relevance threshold is asked about a topic completely absent from the document collection. What does it return?

options.text: Its 5 best-scoring documents anyway, whatever scored highest among a set of irrelevant matches, since top-k alone has no concept of 'not good enough'
An empty result automatically, since nothing is actually relevant
options.why: Without an explicit threshold, top-k has no built-in relevance floor, it always returns exactly k results (or fewer only if the collection itself has fewer than k documents).

options.text: An error, since no document scores above a reasonable bar
options.why: There's no error here, similarity scoring doesn't know what 'reasonable' means without an explicit threshold, it just returns the mathematically highest-scoring k.

questions.question: A retrieval function divides dot product by (magnitude_a × magnitude_b) with no zero check. A document has an all-zero embedding vector. What happens?

options.text: Python raises a ZeroDivisionError right at that division, crashing the whole retrieval call instead of just scoring that one document as irrelevant
The function returns a clear, descriptive 'zero vector' error value automatically, with no explicit guard needed
options.why: Python doesn't do this automatically, dividing by zero is a real, unhandled exception unless you explicitly check for a zero magnitude first and return a defined score instead.

options.text: The document is automatically excluded from results with no other effect
options.why: Without an explicit guard, there's no automatic exclusion, the exception propagates and can crash the entire retrieval call for every document, not just the zero-vector one.

questions.question: What does hybrid search combine, and why?

options.text: Vector similarity search with traditional keyword search, since exact terms (product codes, names) can matter even when their embedding similarity to a paraphrase is unremarkable
Two different embedding models run in parallel for redundancy
options.why: Hybrid search specifically refers to combining vector similarity with KEYWORD search, not running multiple embedding models.

options.text: Retrieval results from two different document collections merged together
options.why: This describes combining data sources, not the vector+keyword scoring combination that defines hybrid search.

questions.question: Chunking guarantees every word ends up in some chunk. Should retrieval guarantee every chunk ends up in some answer?
questions.objective: Decide what completeness means for retrieval vs. chunking

options.text: No, and it shouldn't, chunking's job is completeness (don't lose content), retrieval's job is selectivity (don't include irrelevant content), most chunks correctly never get retrieved for any given query
Yes, otherwise the chunking step was wasted effort
options.why: Chunking effort isn't wasted just because most chunks go unretrieved for any single query, different queries retrieve different chunks over time, that's the system working correctly, not a failure of completeness.

options.text: Yes, retrieval should eventually surface every chunk to some user
options.why: There's no such guarantee or requirement, some content may legitimately never be the best answer to any query asked, that's expected, not a bug.

questions.question: A query about 'resetting a customer password' retrieves a chunk about 'resetting a router to factory settings' with a non-trivial similarity score. Why doesn't this score exactly zero?

options.text: Embeddings capture broad lexical/semantic overlap (like the shared word 'reset'), not topic identity, a modest positive score across unrelated domains is common, not rare
This indicates a bug in the embedding model that needs to be fixed
options.why: This is expected embedding behavior, not a bug, shared vocabulary and phrasing naturally produce some similarity even across different topics.

options.text: It means the two documents are actually about the same topic
options.why: A moderate score from shared terminology doesn't mean the topics are the same, that's exactly the false-positive risk a relevance threshold exists to catch.

questions.question: Four documents score 0.9, 0.3, 0.7, 0.5 in that input order. With k=2 and minScore=0, which are returned, and in what order?
questions.objective: Apply top-k correctly with a partial input order

options.text: The 0.9 and 0.7 documents, sorted with 0.9 first, the two highest scores regardless of original input position
The first two documents in input order (0.9 and 0.3), since top-k just takes the first k results
options.why: Top-k means highest-SCORING k, not first-k-in-input-order, the 0.3 document should not make the cut when 0.7 scored higher.

options.text: All four documents, since minScore=0 means no filtering happens
options.why: minScore=0 does allow all non-negative scores through the FILTER, but k=2 still limits the final OUTPUT to just the top 2 by score.

questions.question: An internal HR-policy chatbot retrieves its best match at similarity 0.31 for a question about parental leave, when the actual policy document exists but uses different wording than the query. The threshold is set at 0.5. What should happen, and is the threshold necessarily wrong?
questions.objective: Apply threshold reasoning to a real knowledge-base search

options.text: The bot should return "no relevant information found" since nothing cleared the threshold, and the threshold isn't necessarily wrong, it may indicate the underlying document needs better wording, phrasing, or a rewritten summary that embeds closer to how people actually ask
The threshold should always be lowered until this specific query's best match clears it
options.why: Tuning the threshold down to force one query's best-but-still-weak match through undermines the threshold for every OTHER query too, a targeted fix (better document phrasing, or a hybrid keyword layer) addresses the specific gap without weakening the general filter.

options.text: The bot should always answer using the best-scoring match regardless of the threshold, since some answer is better than none
options.why: This is exactly the "confidently wrong" failure mode a threshold exists to prevent, a 0.31 similarity score, well below 0.5, isn't a reliable basis for a confident answer.

questions.question: A retrieval function sorts candidates by score, slices to the top 3, THEN filters out anything below the threshold. Five candidates score 0.9, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.05, with threshold 0.4. What does this buggy order return, and how does it differ from filtering first?

options.text: It returns just [0.9] after filtering the sliced top-3 ([0.9, 0.2, 0.15]) down to only what clears 0.4, which happens to match filter-then-slice here, but the bug is real: with a different score distribution, slicing first can permanently discard a candidate that would have cleared the threshold, before filtering ever gets a chance to see it
The two orderings always produce identical results regardless of the score distribution, so the order doesn't actually matter
options.why: The orders coincide on THIS particular input, but they're not equivalent in general, slice-then-filter can only ever return candidates from the pre-filter top-k, permanently losing any lower-ranked-but-still-relevant candidate that a filter-first approach would have kept in consideration.

options.text: Slicing before filtering just returns fewer results faster, with no correctness difference from filtering first
options.why: There is a real correctness difference in general, filtering before slicing guarantees every threshold-clearing candidate is considered before the top-k cut, slicing first can wrongly exclude one earlier.

questions.question: A retrieval system always returns its top-k results even for a query about something the document collection has zero coverage of. What concept in this module is specifically meant to catch that case?
questions.objective: Explain why 'relevant' and 'exists in the collection' aren't the same

options.text: A minimum-relevance threshold, without one the system has no way to say 'nothing here is actually good enough', it just returns whatever scored highest among a set of irrelevant candidates
Chunk overlap, from Module 2, since it's about preserving content at boundaries
options.why: Chunk overlap addresses boundary continuity during ingestion, it has no bearing on whether a QUERY has any relevant match in the collection at all.

options.text: Increasing k so more results are returned, giving a better chance something relevant is included
options.why: Increasing k only returns MORE of the same irrelevant candidates when nothing in the collection is actually relevant, it doesn't introduce any relevance floor, only a threshold does that.

glossary.definition: a vector representing a piece of text's meaning, positioned so similar meanings produce similar vectors.
a score from -1 to 1 measuring the angle between two vectors, ignoring their length.
returning only the k highest-scoring candidates from a ranked search.
a minimum similarity score below which a candidate is excluded, even if it would otherwise make the top-k.
combining vector similarity with keyword search to catch exact-term matches embeddings alone can miss.

project.title: Vector Similarity Search Engine
project.brief: Build a small in-memory vector search engine: cosine similarity, top-k retrieval, and a relevance-threshold cutoff.
